The seismic response characteristics of the alluvial materials underlying therese neighborhoods would have a long period for major earthquakes (Cooper-Clark, 1974), and should not be sympathetic with the response of single-family dwellings. Thus, the level of damage experienced should be less than in more critical locations; however, older structures in these areas could experience more damage due to a lack of basic seismic structural elements. While it is not always economically reasonable to implement structural modifications to existing buildings, it should be possible in the case of wood-frame dwellings. The most important requirement would be to provide bracing or anchorage to the foundation. Some other areas of concern might be seismic stability of chimneys, tile roofs, and water heaters. The 1973 Uniform Building Code contains new measures intended to make structures more resistant to damage from seismic shaking.
Weak and Expansive Soils:
Weak soils have a low shear strength and tend to undergo significant settlement when overloaded with man-made fills or structures. There is frequently a random distribution of weak soils present in alluvial areas. Expansive soils undergo large volume changes with fluctuations of moisture content and may undergo significant strength reduction when saturated.
The Geotechnical Investigation produced mapped expressions of both these soil characteristics. In both cases, the Technical Report cautions that the maps are only as good as the information available when they were compiled and that a certain degree of generalization was necessary in the generation of the maps.
